title: The priest and the big bang
hook: Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, proposed the expanding universe

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laudato si', a pope's letter that opened with a song, and your line was our common home.

A man in a black clerical collar stands at a blackboard covered in equations. He's a Catholic priest, and also a physicist, trained in the mathematics of Einstein's theory of gravity. And the equations are telling him something strange. The universe isn't standing still. It's getting bigger. Run the film backward, he reasons, and everything gets closer and closer together, until it all begins from one small, dense starting point. He called it a primeval atom. Other people later gave it a nickname, and the nickname stuck. His name was Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest.

The first line of the Bible, in the King James translation: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." A few lines later: "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light." It would be easy to hear Lemaître's idea, a universe with a beginning, and say: Genesis, proved by physics. Lemaître himself didn't want anyone to say that. When church voices began to treat his theory as scientific proof of creation, he pushed back, quietly but firmly. His reasoning, as it's usually reported: physics describes how the universe unfolds; it can't tell you whether there is a God. And the Bible wasn't written to teach science; it was written to teach the way to salvation. Keep the two in their own lanes, and neither has to be afraid of the other. He spent his life in both. He said Mass and did mathematics, and didn't think he was being torn in half. Christians have held a range of views on faith and science, and still do. Some read Genesis as a literal account of how the world was made. Others read it as a different kind of truth, about who made the world and why. Lemaître's own path was to study the heavens as closely as he could, and to keep praying. An old psalm sits well beside his blackboard: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." The psalm doesn't do the math. It looks up, and it praises.
screen: `THE HEAVENS DECLARE THE GLORY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Find the sky you have, the night through a window, the daylight and clouds, or the last starry night you remember, and let your eyes go as far as they can; far beyond what you can see, Lemaître would say, the universe is still growing. If you pray, say the psalm's line, the heavens declare the glory of God; if not, simply look, and let yourself be small for a while.
Firmament. The King James word for the sky's dome, named in the psalm that watched beside Georges Lemaître's blackboard as he studied a universe with a beginning.
Your line: faith and science. One priest kept a blackboard and a prayer book both. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians hold a range of views on how scripture and science fit together; the Catholic Church has its own academy of sciences, and Christians work as scientists across many fields.

notes: Claims rule: no dates (1927, 1931, 1951) or numbers given.
Lemaître's objection to Pius XII's 1951 address being read as scientific confirmation of creation is reported in biographies; the script says 'church voices' rather than naming the pope. Confirm.
Lemaître's view that the Bible teaches salvation, not science, is paraphrased from his reported remarks (e.g. his 1933 New York Times interview); confirm the paraphrase.
The nickname 'big bang' is attributed only to 'other people later' (usually credited to Fred Hoyle on BBC radio); confirm.
'trained in the mathematics of Einstein's theory of gravity': he worked with general relativity; confirm phrasing.
Range of Christian views on Genesis and science described without ranking; confirm fairness.
howItsDone mentions the Pontifical Academy of Sciences (of which Lemaître was later president) without naming it; confirm.
